pitfalls: Mixing up the referencing table (S) and the referenced table (R).
cse-1997-a-50.verification: For each operation, checked whether some S tuple can end up with a $d$ value missing from R.

cse-1997-a-51-a.approach: Decode the I/O write cycle to port FFH with one NAND gate: all 8 address bits, $IO/\overline{M}$, and an active-high write strobe (the NOT gate inverts $\overline{WR}$). The NAND output clocks the D flip-flop with $D_3$ on D, and the 8085 reset drives the clear.
cse-1997-a-51-a.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Port | FFH (I/O mapped, `OUT FFH`) |
| Data bit | $D_3$ |
| Parts | 1 NAND (10 inputs), 1 NOT, 1 D flip-flop |
| Clear | on power ON |

steps.title: Which signals identify the cycle
steps.body: For `OUT FFH` the 8085 puts the port address on $A_7$–$A_0$ (copied on $A_{15}$–$A_8$). During the I/O write machine cycle $IO/\overline{M}=1$ and $\overline{WR}=0$. So a write to port FFH means $A_7=\dots=A_0=1$, $IO/\overline{M}=1$ and $WR=1$.

steps.title: Decoder: NAND + NOT
steps.body:
NOT gate: $WR=\overline{\overline{WR}}$. NAND inputs (10): $A_0,\dots,A_7$, $IO/\overline{M}$, $WR$.

$$\text{CLK}=\overline{A_7A_6\cdots A_0\cdot IO/\overline{M}\cdot WR}$$

CLK is low only while the CPU writes to port FFH.

steps.title: Latch the data
steps.body: Connect $D_3$ to the D input and the NAND output to CLK. At the end of the write, $\overline{WR}$ rises, so CLK has a rising edge while $D_3$ is still valid. The flip-flop stores $D_3$, and Q is the 1-bit output port.

steps.title: Clear on power ON
steps.body: Connect the 8085 reset to the flip-flop's clear: RESET OUT (active high) to an active-high CLR, or $\overline{\text{RESET IN}}$ (the power-on RC signal, active low) to an active-low $\overline{\text{CLR}}$. Then Q = 0 after power ON.

answer.value: NAND inputs: $A_0$–$A_7$, $IO/\overline{M}$ and $WR$ (= NOT of $\overline{WR}$). The NAND output clocks the D flip-flop (rising edge at the end of the OUT write cycle). D input = $D_3$. The clear input comes from the 8085 reset (RESET OUT, or $\overline{\text{RESET IN}}$ to an active-low clear), so the flip-flop is cleared at power ON.

pitfalls: Leaving out $IO/\overline{M}$ — a memory write to an address xxFFH would then also clock the port.
Clocking on the falling edge of $\overline{WR}$ — the data is surely stable only at the rising edge.
cse-1997-a-51-a.verification: Counted NAND inputs: 8 address + $IO/\overline{M}$ + $WR$ = 10, matching the fan-in. The NOT gate is used once, for $\overline{WR}$.

cse-1997-a-51-b.approach: Write D3 with `OUT`, flip all bits of A with `CMA`, and jump back. `OUT` (3 machine cycles) + `CMA` (1) + `JMP` (3) = 7 bus cycles between two writes, so ON and OFF each last 7 bus cycles.

steps.title: Program
steps.body:
```
      MVI A, 00H   ; D3 = 0 (any start value)
LOOP: OUT FFH      ; latch D3 into the flip-flop
      CMA          ; complement A, so D3 toggles
      JMP LOOP
```

steps.title: Bus (machine) cycles per loop
steps.body:
| Instruction | Machine cycles |
|---|---|
| `OUT FFH` | opcode fetch, memory read (port no.), I/O write = 3 |
| `CMA` | opcode fetch = 1 |
| `JMP LOOP` | opcode fetch, 2 memory reads = 3 |
| **Total** | $3+1+3=7$ |

steps.title: Time between output changes
steps.body: The output changes only in the I/O write cycle of `OUT`. From one I/O write to the next: CMA (1) + JMP (3) + OUT fetch and read (2) + the new I/O write (1) $= 7$ bus cycles. So each ON and each OFF level lasts 7 bus cycles.

answer.value: `MVI A,00H` ; `LOOP: OUT FFH` ; `CMA` ; `JMP LOOP` — 3 + 1 + 3 = 7 bus cycles per half-period.

pitfalls: Counting T-states instead of bus (machine) cycles.
Putting `MVI` inside the loop — it adds 2 cycles and stops the toggling.
cse-1997-a-51-b.verification: Cycles from write to write: CMA 1, JMP 3, OUT fetch 1, OUT read 1, write 1 → 7.

cse-1997-a-52.approach: Recursive pairwise swap: for nodes $p$ (1st) and $q$ (2nd), $q$ becomes the head, $q$ points to $p$, and $p$ points to the swapped rest of the list starting at $t=q\uparrow.next$.

steps.title: Base cases (lines 4–5)
steps.body: Empty list: return `p` (nil). One node: nothing to swap, so the line 5 box is **`p`**.

steps.title: Name the pieces (lines 7, 9)
steps.body: `q := p↑.next` is the 2nd node; `t := q↑.next` is the rest of the list, starting at node 3.

scene.caption: p = a1, q = a2, t = a3

steps.title: New head (line 8)
steps.body: After the swap $a_2$ comes first, so line 8 is **`change := q`**. In Pascal the function result may be assigned before the end.

steps.title: Relink (lines 10–11)
steps.body: Line 10: **`q↑.next := p`** ($a_2\to a_1$). Line 11: **`p↑.next := change(t)`** ($a_1\to$ the swapped remainder). `t` was saved on line 9 before line 10 overwrote `q↑.next`.

scene.caption: Result for n = 5: a2 a1 a4 a3 a5

pitfalls: Writing `change := t` on line 8 — the new head must be $a_2$.
Overwriting `q↑.next` before saving `t` — the rest of the list would be lost (the given line order avoids this).

cse-1997-a-53-a.approach: There are $n^2$ vertices, so a spanning tree has $n^2-1$ edges. Every edge weighs $1$ (horizontal or vertical) or $\sqrt2$ (diagonal). The unit edges alone connect the grid, so the MST uses only weight-1 edges.

steps.title: Edge weights
steps.body: Adjacent points differ by at most 1 in each coordinate: horizontal and vertical edges weigh $1$, diagonal edges weigh $\sqrt2$.

steps.title: Lower bound and construction
steps.body: Any spanning tree has $n^2-1$ edges, each of weight $\ge1$, so its weight is $\ge n^2-1$. A "comb" of unit edges (each row joined horizontally, plus the first column joined vertically) is a spanning tree with exactly $n^2-1$ unit edges.

pitfalls: Counting $n^2$ edges instead of $n^2-1$.

cse-1997-a-53-b.approach: Use as many $\sqrt2$ (diagonal) edges as possible. A diagonal step keeps the parity of $x+y$, so diagonal edges form two classes (the two checkerboard colours). A tree on each class uses $n^2-2$ diagonals, and one unit edge joins the two.

steps.title: Diagonals keep the colour
steps.body: A diagonal step changes both $x$ and $y$ by $\pm1$, so $x+y$ keeps its parity. Diagonal edges never join an "even" point to an "odd" one. So a spanning tree contains at most $n^2-2$ diagonals and at least one unit edge between the two classes.

steps.title: Both classes are diagonal-connected
steps.body: For $n\ge2$, each colour class is connected by diagonal moves (for $n=2$: $(1,1)-(2,2)$ and $(1,2)-(2,1)$; larger boards work the same way). So each class has a spanning tree of diagonals: $(\#\text{even}-1)+(\#\text{odd}-1)=n^2-2$ edges.

steps.title: Join and total
steps.body:
One unit edge joins the two trees, giving $n^2-1$ edges in all:
$$w_{\max}=(n^2-2)\sqrt2+1$$

pitfalls: Answering $(n^2-1)\sqrt2$ — diagonal edges alone cannot join the two colour classes.

cse-1997-a-54-a-i.approach: Trace the recursion. With call by value $z$ stays 10 on the way down; the assignments $z:=x+10$ run on the way back, innermost first, so the outermost frame writes last.

steps.title: Going down (z stays 10)
steps.body:
With call by value each call has its own $x$. $z$ changes only on the way back, so on the way down every call adds $z=10$:

| call | $x$ on entry | $x\le40$? | $x:=x+z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | yes | 20 |
| 2 | 20 | yes | 30 |
| 3 | 30 | yes | 40 |
| 4 | 40 | yes | 50 |
| 5 | 50 | no | — |

steps.title: Coming back (z overwritten)
steps.body:
Each frame sets $z:=x+10$ with its **own** $x$, from the innermost frame outwards:
- call 4: $z=50+10=60$
- call 3: $z=40+10=50$
- call 2: $z=30+10=40$
- call 1: $z=20+10=30$

The outermost call writes last, so $z=30$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Printed value $= 30$. (`recur` is called 5 times, with arguments 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.)

animation.caption: z := 10, then recur(z)

pitfalls: Taking the innermost assignment ($z=60$) as final — the outer frames write after it.
cse-1997-a-54-a-i.verification: Frame $x$ values after the update are 20, 30, 40, 50; the last assignment made is $20+10=30$.

cse-1997-a-54-a-ii.approach: Count calls in the same call-by-value trace: the argument goes $10\to20\to30\to40\to50$, and the call with 50 fails the test and stops.

steps.title: Arguments of successive calls
steps.body: $z=10$ during the descent, so each call passes $x+10$ to the next: arguments $10, 20, 30, 40, 50$.

steps.title: Stopping call
steps.body: The call with $x=50$ fails $x\le40$ and returns without recursing. Total calls $=5$, counting this last call.

pitfalls: Answering 4 by leaving out the last call, which fails the test but is still a call.
cse-1997-a-54-a-ii.verification: Same table as part (i): calls 1–5, of which the first four recurse.

cse-1997-a-54-b.approach: With call by reference, $x$ is another name for the global $z$, so every update of $x$ changes $z$ immediately. Trace the one shared value.

scene.caption: x aliases z; z doubled to 80

steps.title: Result
steps.body: `writeln(z)` prints $110$.

animation.caption: z := 10, then recur(z)

pitfalls: Forgetting that $x:=x+z$ doubles $z$ when $x$ and $z$ are the same variable.

cse-1997-a-55-a.approach: Count the letters each production adds. With $a$ uses of $S\to bSe$ and $p,q,r$ uses of the recursive rules of $P,Q,R$, the string is $b^{a+p}c^{p+q}d^{q+r}e^{r+a}$. Then eliminate the parameters.

steps.title: Shape of every string
steps.body:
$S\Rightarrow^* b^aSe^a\Rightarrow b^aPQRe^a$, with $P\Rightarrow^* b^pc^p$, $Q\Rightarrow^*c^qd^q$, $R\Rightarrow^*d^re^r$. So
$$i=a+p,\; j=p+q,\; k=q+r,\; m=r+a.$$

steps.title: Eliminate the parameters
steps.body: $i+k=a+p+q+r=j+m$. So every generated string has $i+k=j+m$.

steps.title: Every such string is generated
steps.body: Given $i+k=j+m$, take $a=\max(0,i-j)$, $p=i-a$, $q=j-p$, $r=k-q$. All are $\ge0$, and $r+a=k-j+i=m$. So the condition is also sufficient.

pitfalls: Answering $i=m$ and $j=k$ — that misses strings such as $bccd$ ($i=1,j=2,k=1,m=0$).
cse-1997-a-55-a.verification: $bccd$: $a=0,p=1,q=1,r=0$ derives it, and $1+1=2+0$ ✓. $bbccdd$ ($i=j=k=2$, $m=0$): $4\ne2$, and it cannot be derived.

cse-1997-a-55-b.approach: Two parse trees exist when the same $(i,j,k,m)$ comes from two parameter tuples $(a,p,q,r)$. Find the smallest string for which two values of $a$ are possible.

steps.title: When two trees exist
steps.body: From $p=i-a$, $q=j-i+a$, $r=m-a$, each value of $a$ fixes the whole derivation. Two values of $a$ are possible iff $\max(0,i-j)<\min(i,m)$. This needs $i\ge1$, $m\ge1$ and $j\ge1$ (if $j=0$ then $i-j=i$, so the range is empty).

steps.title: Smallest choice
steps.body: $i=j=m=1$ gives $k=j+m-i=1$: the string $bcde$ (length 4). Shorter strings ($\varepsilon$, $be$, $bc$, $cd$, $de$) have only one possible $a$.

steps.title: The two trees
steps.body:
1. $S\Rightarrow bSe\Rightarrow bPQRe\Rightarrow b\,(cQd)\,e\Rightarrow bcde$ ($a=1$, $q=1$).
2. $S\Rightarrow PQR\Rightarrow (bPc)(\varepsilon)(dRe)\Rightarrow bcde$ ($a=0$, $p=r=1$).

pitfalls: Proposing $be$ — it has only the derivation $S\Rightarrow bSe$ with $PQR\Rightarrow\varepsilon$.
cse-1997-a-55-b.verification: Checked every string of length ≤ 2 in the language: each has exactly one parameter tuple.

cse-1997-b-56-a.approach: Each insertion misses bucket 1 with probability $(n-1)/n$, independently of the others.
cse-1997-b-56-a.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Buckets | $n$, each with probability $1/n$ |
| Insertions | $K$ distinct keys, independent |

steps.title: One insertion
steps.body: $P(\text{key avoids bucket 1}) = 1-\frac1n = \frac{n-1}{n}$.

steps.title: All K insertions
steps.body: $$P = \left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^K$$

pitfalls: Using $1-K/n$, which treats the events as disjoint.

cse-1997-b-56-b.approach: No collision means all $K$ keys land in distinct buckets (the birthday problem). The $i$-th key must avoid the $i-1$ buckets already used.
cse-1997-b-56-b.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Buckets | $n$, each with probability $1/n$ |
| Insertions | $K$ distinct keys, independent |

steps.title: Key by key
steps.body: Key $i$ avoids the $i-1$ occupied buckets with probability $\frac{n-i+1}{n}$.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: $$P=\prod_{i=1}^{K}\frac{n-i+1}{n}=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-K+1)}{n^K}=\frac{n!}{(n-K)!\,n^K}$$ For $K>n$ a collision is certain, so $P=0$ (the product contains the factor $0$).

pitfalls: Writing $\binom nK/n^K$ — the order of insertions matters.

cse-1997-b-56-c.approach: The first collision is at insertion $K$ when the first $K-1$ keys go to distinct buckets and the $K$-th key hits one of those $K-1$ occupied buckets.
cse-1997-b-56-c.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Buckets | $n$, each with probability $1/n$ |
| Insertions | $K$ distinct keys, independent |

steps.title: First K−1 distinct
steps.body: Part (b) with $K-1$ keys: $\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-K+2)}{n^{K-1}}$.

steps.title: K-th key collides
steps.body:
Exactly $K-1$ buckets are occupied, so $P(\text{hit}) = \frac{K-1}{n}$. Multiply:
$$P=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-K+2)}{n^{K-1}}\cdot\frac{K-1}{n}$$

pitfalls: Using $1-P(\text{no collision in }K)$ — that is "at least one collision by $K$", not "first collision at $K$".
cse-1997-b-56-c.verification: Equals $P_{\text{none}}(K-1)-P_{\text{none}}(K)$; for $n=2,K=2$: $1-\frac12=\frac12$, and the formula gives $\frac{2}{2}\cdot\frac12=\frac12$ ✓. $K=1$ gives 0 ✓.

cse-1997-b-57-a.approach: A one-to-one function picks a distinct image for each of the n domain elements in order, so count ordered selections of n out of m values: the falling factorial $m^{\underline n}$.

steps.title: Assign images in order
steps.body: $f(1)$ has $m$ choices, $f(2)$ has $m-1$ (must differ from $f(1)$), …, $f(n)$ has $m-n+1$ choices.

pitfalls: $m^n$ counts all functions, not just one-to-one ones.
$\binom{m}{n}$ ignores which domain element gets which image (that is part (c)).
cse-1997-b-57-a.verification: Check $m=3,n=2$: injective maps $\{1,2\}\to\{1,2,3\}$ are the 6 ordered pairs of distinct values, and $3!/1!=6$.

cse-1997-b-57-b.approach: Since $f$ is one-to-one, at most one $i$ maps to 1. Choose that $i$, then map the remaining $n-1$ elements injectively into the remaining $m-1$ values.

steps.title: Pick the preimage of 1
steps.body: Exactly one $i$ has $f(i)=1$ (injectivity forbids two). There are $n$ choices for $i$.

steps.title: Map the rest
steps.body:
The other $n-1$ domain elements go one-to-one into $\{2,\dots,m\}$ ($m-1$ values):
$$\frac{(m-1)!}{\big((m-1)-(n-1)\big)!}=\frac{(m-1)!}{(m-n)!}$$

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body:
$$n\cdot\frac{(m-1)!}{(m-n)!}$$
Equivalently, total minus those avoiding 1: $\frac{m!}{(m-n)!}-\frac{(m-1)!}{(m-1-n)!}$ (for $m>n$).

pitfalls: Do not multiply by more than $n$ — no two elements can both map to 1.

cse-1997-b-57-c.approach: A strictly increasing function is determined completely by its image set: any $n$-element subset of $\{1..m\}$, listed in increasing order, gives exactly one such $f$.

steps.title: Bijection with subsets
steps.body: If $f(1)<f(2)<\dots<f(n)$, the image is an $n$-subset of $\{1,\dots,m\}$. Conversely each $n$-subset, sorted, defines exactly one increasing $f$.

steps.title: Count subsets
steps.body:
$$\binom{m}{n}=\frac{m!}{n!\,(m-n)!}$$
(Equivalently: each image set appears in $n!$ injective functions, and exactly one of those orders is increasing: $\frac{m!/(m-n)!}{n!}$.)

pitfalls: Answering $m!/(m-n)!$ counts all orders of the chosen images, not only the increasing one.

cse-1997-b-58-a.approach: Check reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of $E$ directly, each one inherited from a property of $R$ (reflexive, the symmetric definition of $E$, transitive).

steps.title: Reflexive
steps.body: For every $a\in A$, $(a,a)\in R$ since $R$ is reflexive. Both conditions of $E$ hold with $b=a$, so $(a,a)\in E$.

steps.title: Symmetric
steps.body: If $(a,b)\in E$ then $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,a)\in R$. The same two facts read in the other order say $(b,a)\in E$.

steps.title: Transitive
steps.body: Let $(a,b)\in E$ and $(b,c)\in E$. Then $(a,b),(b,c)\in R\Rightarrow(a,c)\in R$ and $(c,b),(b,a)\in R\Rightarrow(c,a)\in R$ by transitivity of $R$. Hence $(a,c)\in E$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $E$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation on $A$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Proof: $E$ is reflexive (from $R$ reflexive), symmetric (its definition is symmetric in $a,b$) and transitive (apply transitivity of $R$ in both directions).

pitfalls: Transitivity must be shown for both $(a,c)$ and $(c,a)$ — it needs transitivity of $R$ twice.
cse-1997-b-58-a.verification: Example: $R=\le$ on integers gives $E$ = equality, an equivalence relation, as expected.

cse-1997-b-58-b.approach: First show the relation does not depend on the chosen representatives (so $E_1\le E_2$ iff $(a,b)\in R$ for ALL $a\in E_1,b\in E_2$), then reflexivity and transitivity come from $R$ and antisymmetry from the definition of $E$.

steps.title: Representatives do not matter
steps.body: Suppose $(a,b)\in R$ with $a\in E_1,b\in E_2$, and take any $a'\in E_1,b'\in E_2$. Then $(a',a)\in R$ and $(b,b')\in R$ (definition of $E$), so by transitivity $(a',a),(a,b),(b,b')\in R\Rightarrow (a',b')\in R$.

steps.title: Reflexive
steps.body: For a class $E_1$ pick $a\in E_1$; $(a,a)\in R$, so $E_1\le E_1$.

steps.title: Antisymmetric
steps.body: Let $E_1\le E_2$ and $E_2\le E_1$. Take $a\in E_1,b\in E_2$; by the first step $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,a)\in R$, so $(a,b)\in E$: $a$ and $b$ are in the same class, i.e. $E_1=E_2$.

steps.title: Transitive
steps.body: Let $E_1\le E_2$, $E_2\le E_3$. Fix $a\in E_1,b\in E_2,c\in E_3$; by the first step $(a,b),(b,c)\in R$, so $(a,c)\in R$, giving $E_1\le E_3$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $\le$ is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on the equivalence classes of $E$: a partial order. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Proof: $\le$ is well defined independent of representatives; reflexive from $R$ reflexive, transitive from $R$ transitive, and antisymmetric because mutual $R$-relation puts elements in the same $E$-class.

pitfalls: Without the representative-independence step, transitivity fails: the witnesses $b$ for $E_1\le E_2$ and $E_2\le E_3$ may differ.
Antisymmetry needs $E_1=E_2$ as classes, not $a=b$ as elements.
cse-1997-b-58-b.verification: Collapsing the cycles of a preorder (e.g. reachability in a directed graph → its condensation DAG) gives exactly this partial order.

cse-1997-b-59-a.approach: $F$ counts monotone lattice paths: $F(n,m)=\binom{n+m}{n}$, which satisfies both the base case and Pascal's rule. Put $m=2$.

steps.title: Guess the closed form
steps.body: Try $G(n,m)=\binom{n+m}{n}$. Base: if $n=0$ or $m=0$, $G=\binom{m}{0}$ or $\binom{n}{n}=1$ ✓.

steps.title: Check the recurrence
steps.body: With $N=n+m$, $k=n$: $\binom{N}{n}=\binom{N-1}{n}+\binom{N-1}{n-1}=G(n,m-1)+G(n-1,m)$ ✓. So $F=G$.

cse-1997-b-59-b.approach: Match the recurrence to Pascal's rule: $\binom{n+m}{n}$ equals 1 when either argument is 0 and splits exactly as $F$ does.

steps.title: Recursive case
steps.body:
$$\binom{n+m}{n}=\binom{n+m-1}{n}+\binom{n+m-1}{n-1}=\binom{n+(m-1)}{n}+\binom{(n-1)+m}{n-1}$$
which is $F(n,m-1)+F(n-1,m)$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: $$F(n,m)=\binom{n+m}{n}=\frac{(n+m)!}{n!\,m!}$$

cse-1997-b-59-b.shortcut: $F(n,m)$ counts paths from $(n,m)$ to an axis taking unit steps left/down — the classic $\binom{n+m}{n}$ grid-path count.

cse-1997-b-59-c.approach: Write the call-count recurrence $C(n,m)=1+C(n-1,m)+C(n,m-1)$ with $C=1$ at the base, and notice $C=2F-1$ satisfies it (a full binary recursion tree with $F$ leaves has $2F-1$ nodes).
concepts: Full binary tree: leaves vs nodes

steps.title: Call-count recurrence
steps.body: Base ($n\le0$ or $m\le0$): $C=1$. Otherwise $C(n,m)=1+C(n-1,m)+C(n,m-1)$.

cse-1997-b-59-c.shortcut: Every non-base call has exactly 2 children, so the recursion tree is a full binary tree; its leaves each return 1, so #leaves $=F(n,m)$ and #nodes $=2F-1$.
pitfalls: Counting only the leaves ($F$) or forgetting the original call.

cse-1997-b-60-a.approach: Strong induction on $h$: a tree of height $h$ has one subtree of height $h-1$ (≥ $2^{h-1}$ nodes); the balance condition forces the other subtree to have at least $2^{h-1}-1$ nodes.

steps.title: Base h = 0
steps.body: A tree of height 0 is a single node: $1=2^0$ nodes ✓.

steps.title: Hypothesis
steps.body: Assume every size-balanced tree of height $h-1$ has at least $2^{h-1}$ nodes ($h\ge1$). Every subtree of a size-balanced tree is itself size-balanced.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body:
A tree $T$ of height $h$ has a subtree $T_1$ of height exactly $h-1$, so $|T_1|\ge2^{h-1}$. The other subtree $T_2$ satisfies $\big||T_1|-|T_2|\big|\le1$, so $|T_2|\ge2^{h-1}-1$.
$$|T|=1+|T_1|+|T_2|\ge1+2^{h-1}+2^{h-1}-1=2^h$$

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: By induction every size-balanced binary tree of height $h$ has at least $2^h$ nodes. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Proof by induction: base $h=0$ gives 1 node; for height $h$, one subtree has ≥ $2^{h-1}$ nodes and the other ≥ $2^{h-1}-1$, so total ≥ $1+2^{h-1}+2^{h-1}-1=2^h$.

pitfalls: The second subtree may have height less than $h-1$ — bound it through the size condition, not its height.
cse-1997-b-60-a.verification: The bound is tight: a perfect tree of height $h-1$ plus one extra leaf has $2^h$ nodes and is size-balanced.

cse-1997-b-60-b.approach: A size-balanced tree is complete except possibly the last level, so level $h-1$ is full: $2^{h-1}$ nodes.

steps.title: Levels above the last are full
steps.body: By induction: the subtrees of the root have sizes $k$ and $k$ or $k+1$. If their heights differ, the shorter one (height $h-2$, < $2^{h-1}$ nodes) and taller one (≥ $2^{h-1}$ nodes, part (a)) differ in size by 1, which forces sizes $2^{h-1}-1$ and $2^{h-1}$ — the shorter is perfect. So in every case all levels $0..h-1$ are full.

steps.title: Count level h − 1
steps.body: A full level at distance $h-1$ in a binary tree has $2^{h-1}$ nodes.

cse-1997-b-61.approach: This is the two-pointer sliding window over positive numbers: keep $sum=A[i]+\dots+A[j]$; extend $j$ while $sum<M$, shrink from $i$ (recording the length) once $sum\ge M$.

steps.title: Invariant
steps.body: Window is $A[i..j]$ and $sum=\sum_{k=i}^{j}A[k]$. Initially $i=j=1$, so **line 3:** `Sum := A[1]`.

steps.title: Decide: grow or shrink
steps.body: Lines 7–11 extend the window (advance $j$), which is needed only when the window is too small. So **line 6:** `If sum < M then`. The else-branch (lines 15–17) runs when $sum\ge M$: it records length $j-i+1$ via $min=j-i$ and drops $A[i]$.

steps.title: Maintain the sum
steps.body: After `j := j + 1` the new element enters the window: **line 11:** `sum := sum + A[j]`.

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body: Because all $A[k]>0$, shrinking a window with $sum\ge M$ is the only way to find a shorter one, and growing is the only way to reach $M$. If no window ever reaches $M$, $min$ stays $n$ and $n+1$ is printed.

pitfalls: Line 6 as `sum >= M` swaps the meaning of the two branches.
Line 11 must add $A[j]$ after $j$ is incremented, not $A[j+1]$.
cse-1997-b-61.verification: Trace $A=[1,4,2],M=5$: sum=1<5 → j=2,sum=5 ≥5 → min=1, sum=4,i=2 → <5 → j=3,sum=6 → min stays 1, sum=2,i=3 → <5, j=n → finish; prints 2 (window [1,4] or [4,2]) ✓.

cse-1997-b-63-a.approach: S1 runs once per iteration of the while loop, and $t_2$ walks from the 2nd node to past the last node exactly once.

steps.title: Loop range
steps.body: $t_2$ starts at node 2 and moves one node per iteration (`t2 = t2->next` is unconditional) until it becomes NULL after node $n$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Iterations for nodes $2,3,\dots,n$: $n-1$. S1 is evaluated once per iteration, so $n-1$ comparisons. Note: the printed code writes `t1.val`/`t2.val`; read them as `t1->val`/`t2->val`.

cse-1997-b-63-b.approach: S2 executes once for every new distinct value met after the first node, so it ranges from 0 (all equal) to $n-1$ (all distinct).

steps.title: When S2 runs
steps.body: S2 runs exactly when $t_2$ holds a value different from the last kept node $t_1$ — i.e. at each position where the sorted list changes value.

steps.title: Minimum
steps.body: All $n$ elements equal: S1 is false every time → S2 runs **0** times.

steps.title: Maximum
steps.body: All elements distinct: S1 is true in all $n-1$ iterations → S2 runs **$n-1$** times.

cse-1997-b-63-c.approach: `*j` starts at 1 for the head and is incremented once per S2 (each new distinct value kept), so it ends as the number of distinct elements — the length of the de-duplicated list.

steps.title: Invariant
steps.body: After `*j = 1`, `*j` equals the number of nodes kept so far (head, then every node linked by `t1->next = t2`).

steps.title: At the end
steps.body: Kept nodes = one per distinct value, so `*j` = number of distinct elements = length of the resulting list (0 for an empty list, 1 for a single node).

answer.value: Number of distinct elements in the list (length of the resulting list)

cse-1997-b-64-a.approach: Count child pointers two ways: every node except the root is someone's child, and a node with $M$ keys has $M+1$ children.

steps.title: Children total
steps.body: Let $I$ = number of internal nodes. Every node except the root is a child of an internal node: total children $=(I+l)-1$.

steps.title: Keys total
steps.body: Node $x$ with $M_x$ keys has $M_x+1$ children, so $\sum M_x=\sum(\text{children}_x)-I=(I+l-1)-I=l-1$.

cse-1997-b-64-a.verification: A root with 1 key and 2 leaves: $l=2$, keys $=1=l-1$ ✓.

cse-1997-b-64-b.approach: To maximise internal nodes, give every node the minimum fan-out: non-root internal nodes need ≥ 4 keys = 5 children, root ≥ 2 children. Build level by level from the 52 leaves.

| Node | Keys | Children |

| non-root internal | 4 – 8 | 5 – 9 |
| root | 1 – 8 | 2 – 9 |

steps.body: Each needs 5–9 children. Max nodes $=\lfloor52/5\rfloor=10$ (e.g. eight with 5 children, two with 6: $40+12=52$).

steps.title: Can the root sit on top?
steps.body: 10 children need 9 keys > $2d=8$, so no. Add a level: $\lfloor10/5\rfloor=2$ nodes of 5 children each.

steps.title: Root

2 children (1 key) is allowed for the root.
$$10+2+1=13$$

Forgetting the root may have as few as 2 children.
cse-1997-b-64-b.verification: Any other split has ≤ 10 nodes above the leaves and then ≤ 2 above them, so 13 is the maximum.

cse-1997-b-64-c.approach: Minimise fan-out at every level: the root has at least 2 children and every other internal node at least $d+1$ children; leaves are all at depth $h$.

steps.body: Depth 0: 1 root. Depth 1: ≥ 2 nodes. Each internal node at depth $1..h-1$ has ≥ $d+1$ children, so depth $k$ has ≥ $2(d+1)^{k-1}$ nodes.

Giving the root $d+1$ children — it may have only 2.

cse-1997-b-65.approach: Track two counters at once: $\#a \bmod 2$ and $\#b \bmod 3$. The product of a 2-state and a 3-state DFA gives 6 states, and all 6 are pairwise distinguishable, so 6 is minimum.

steps.title: States
steps.body: State $(i,j)$ means $\#a\equiv i \pmod 2$, $\#b\equiv j\pmod 3$: six states $(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2)$. Start = final = $(0,0)$.

scene.caption: Start state (0,0) is also the only accepting state.

steps.title: Transitions
steps.body:
| | on a | on b |
|---|---|---|
| $(i,j)$ | $(1-i,\,j)$ | $(i,\,(j+1)\bmod 3)$ |
The a-edges flip the row; the b-edges cycle along a row.

scene.caption: a toggles the a-parity (vertical), b advances the b-count mod 3 (horizontal cycle).

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: Two different states $(i,j)\ne(i',j')$ are distinguished by the suffix $a^{(2-i)\bmod2}b^{(3-j)\bmod3}$, which takes $(i,j)$ to $(0,0)$ (accept) but $(i',j')$ elsewhere (reject). So no two states merge: **6 states** is minimum.

answer.value: 6-state DFA: states $(i,j)$ with $i=\#a \bmod 2$, $j=\#b \bmod 3$; start and only final state $(0,0)$; on a: $(i,j)\to(1-i,j)$; on b: $(i,j)\to(i,(j+1)\bmod 3)$.

pitfalls: Building the two machines in sequence (concatenation) instead of in parallel (product).
Using 5 states (2+3) — that cannot remember both counts.

cse-1997-b-66.approach: Modify a DFA $M=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$ for $L$. For prefixes, accept wherever an accepting state is still reachable; for reversal, flip every edge and swap start/final roles, giving an NFA.

steps.title: L^P: construction
steps.body: Let $F'=\{q\in Q : \exists w,\ \hat\delta(q,w)\in F\}$ (states that can still reach $F$). $M^P=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F')$.

steps.title: L^P: correctness
steps.body: $s\in L(M^P)\iff \hat\delta(q_0,s)\in F'\iff\exists s'\,:\,\hat\delta(q_0,ss')\in F\iff \exists s'\,:\,ss'\in L\iff s\in L^P$. $F'$ is computable by graph reachability, so $M^P$ is a finite automaton.

steps.title: L^R: construction
steps.body: Build NFA $N$: same states plus a new start $p_0$; for each $\delta(q,a)=r$ add the reversed edge $r\xrightarrow{a}q$; add $p_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f$ for every $f\in F$; the only final state is $q_0$.

steps.title: L^R: correctness
steps.body: $N$ has a path from $f\in F$ to $q_0$ labelled $a_k\cdots a_1$ exactly when $M$ has a path $q_0\to f$ labelled $a_1\cdots a_k$. So $N$ accepts $w^R$ iff $M$ accepts $w$, i.e. $L(N)=L^R$. By subset construction an NFA has an equivalent DFA, so $L^R$ is accepted by a finite state machine. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: For $L^P$: in the DFA for $L$, make final every state from which some final state is reachable. For $L^R$: reverse all transitions, make the old start state the only final state, and add a new start state with ε-moves to the old final states (an NFA, hence convertible to a DFA).

pitfalls: Making every state final for $L^P$ — dead states must stay non-final.
Reversing edges of a DFA gives an NFA in general; you must invoke subset construction (or NFA acceptance) to finish.
cse-1997-b-66.verification: $L=\{ab\}$: $L^P=\{\varepsilon,a,ab\}$ (states before the dead state become final) and $L^R=\{ba\}$ from the reversed path ✓.

cse-1997-b-67.approach: Encode precedence and associativity in the grammar levels: statements on top, `<` (lowest precedence, non-associative) above `+` (left-associative) above operands, and a left-recursive statement list for `begin … end`.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
```
S  → id := E
   | while E do S
   | begin SL end
SL → SL ; S | S
```
Each statement starts with a distinct token (`id`, `while`, `begin`), and `while … do S` has no `else`, so there is no dangling ambiguity.

steps.title: Expressions
steps.body:
```
E → T < T | T
T → T + F | F
F → id | num | ( E )
```
`<` sits at the lowest level (non-associative as in Pascal; `E → E < T | T` would also be unambiguous). `T → T + F` makes `+` left-associative and binds tighter than `<`.

steps.title: Why unambiguous
steps.body: Every expression has a unique split: the (at most one) top-level `<`, then the last top-level `+` in each side. Statement lists split only at `;` with left recursion, so each string has exactly one parse tree.

answer.value: S → id := E | while E do S | begin SL end;  SL → SL ; S | S;  E → T < T | T (or E → E < T | T);  T → T + F | F;  F → id | num | ( E )

pitfalls: Writing `E → E + E | E < E | id` is ambiguous (both precedence and associativity).
`SL → S ; SL | S ; SL` style rules with an empty alternative can create ambiguity with trailing `;`.
cse-1997-b-67.verification: `a + b < c + d` has the unique tree $(a+b) < (c+d)$; `a + b + c` parses only as $(a+b)+c$.

steps.title: Leaves
Multiplication and addition
Assignment
steps.body:
```
assign-stmt → LHS := E
   { assign.code := LHS.code || E.code || '(:=,' || LHS.type || ')' }
```
The assignment operator is typed by the target variable.

steps.title: Example
steps.body:
With `x:real, a,b:int`, `x := a + b * x` gives
`x a b x (*,r) (+,r) (:=,r)` — `b*x` is real because `x` is real, so the sum is real too.

Typing the assignment by the expression instead of the target variable.

cse-1997-b-69.approach: Enumerate the only call chains the program allows. C makes no calls, so a chain through C stops at 4 records; the only way to have 5 records is Main → A → B → A → B. Then set each static link by lexical nesting and each dynamic link to the caller.

steps.title: Possible call chains
steps.body:
Calls that exist: Main→A, A→B, B→C, B→A. C calls nothing.

- Main, A, B, C — only **4** records, and C cannot extend it.
- Main, A, B, A, B — **5** records.

So the stack (bottom → top) is **Main, A, B, A, B**; the top is the second activation of B.

steps.title: Main calls A, A calls B
steps.body: Push A (local $Y$) and then B (local $Z$). A is nested directly in Main, so A's static link → Main; B is nested in A, so B's static link → the A that called it.

steps.title: B calls A, A calls B
steps.body: B calls A (recursion through B). A is declared in Main, so the new A's static link → **Main**, while its dynamic link → **B₁** (the caller). A₂ then calls B: B₂'s static and dynamic links both → **A₂**.

scene.caption: Five records: Main, A, B, A, B

steps.title: Run-time stack
steps.body:
| Record (bottom → top) | Locals | Static link | Dynamic link |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main | X | — | — |
| A₁ | Y | Main | Main |
| B₁ | Z | A₁ | A₁ |
| A₂ | Y | Main | B₁ |
| B₂ (**top**) | Z | A₂ | A₂ |

C's own $Z$ never appears because C is not active.

pitfalls: Setting A₂'s static link to B₁ — static links follow declaration nesting, not the caller.
Including C: a chain through C has only 4 records and C calls nothing.

cse-1997-b-70-a.approach: Mealy-machine minimisation by partition refinement: start with blocks of equal output pairs (P₁), then repeatedly split blocks whose members go to different blocks on some input, until nothing changes.

steps.title: Split by outputs
steps.body:
Output pairs (input 0, input 1): A, B, E, F, G give $(1,1)$; C, D, H give $(0,1)$.

$P_1=\{A,B,E,F,G\},\ \{C,D,H\}$

steps.title: Refine to P₃
steps.body:
Under $P_2$:

- A: B → AB, H → CDH; B: F → EFG, D → CDH ⇒ A, B split.
- E, F, G all go to (CDH, CDH) ⇒ stay.
- C: D → CDH, E → EFG; D: C → CDH, F → EFG; H: C → CDH, A → AB ⇒ H splits off.

$P_3=\{A\},\{B\},\{C,D\},\{E,F,G\},\{H\}$

steps.title: Check stability
steps.body:
Under $P_3$: C → (D, E) = (CD, EFG), D → (C, F) = (CD, EFG) — same. E → (D, C), F → (C, C), G → (C, D) all = (CD, CD) — same. No block splits, so $P_4=P_3$ is the equivalence partition:

$$\{A\},\ \{B\},\ \{C,D\},\ \{E,F,G\},\ \{H\}$$

pitfalls: Stopping after the output split — A and B have the same outputs but are not equivalent.
Merging H with C, D: H goes to A on input 1, which is in a different block.
cse-1997-b-70-a.verification: One more refinement pass under the final partition produced no split.

steps.body: Equivalent classes: $A$, $B$, $CD$, $EFG$, $H$. Class map: C, D → CD; E, F, G → EFG.

| A | B, 1 | H, 1 |
| B | EFG, 1 | CD, 1 |
| CD | CD, 0 | EFG, 1 |
| EFG | CD, 1 | CD, 1 |
| H | CD, 0 | A, 1 |

5 states instead of 8.

cse-1997-b-71-a.approach: Pair the clauses with the distributive law $(a+b)(a+c)=a+bc$: the $w$-clauses and the $x$-clauses each collapse, and the middle clause is then absorbed.

steps.title: Collapse clause pairs
steps.body:
$(\overline{w}+y)(\overline{w}+z)=\overline{w}+yz$ and $(\overline{x}+y)(\overline{x}+z)=\overline{x}+yz$.

So $f=(\overline{w}+yz)(\overline{x}+yz)(w+\overline{x}+z)=(\overline{w}\,\overline{x}+yz)(w+\overline{x}+z)$.

steps.title: Absorb the last clause
steps.body:
$\overline{w}\,\overline{x}\cdot(w+\overline{x}+z)=\overline{w}\,\overline{x}$ (contains $\overline{x}$) and $yz\cdot(w+\overline{x}+z)=yz$ (contains $z$).

$$f=\overline{w}\,\overline{x}+yz$$

steps.body: On the K-map the 1s are $m_0,m_1,m_2,m_3,m_7,m_{11},m_{15}$. Both quads are essential prime implicants and together cover all 7 ones, so $f=\overline{w}\,\overline{x}+yz$ is the minimal SOP.

$4+4-1=7$ input combinations.

cse-1997-b-72-a.given: $f$: 6 bits = sign + 5 magnitude bits (a fraction). $e$: 4 bits = sign + 3 magnitude bits. $n = f \cdot 2^{e}$. $A = 54.75$, $B = 9.75$.

steps.title: Fit A into the fields
steps.body:
Five magnitude bits: $11011$ (the dropped bits $011$ are lost by truncation). $e = 6 = 110_2$.

$f_A = 0\ 11011$, $e_A = 0\ 110$; stored value $0.11011_2 \times 2^6 = \tfrac{27}{32} \times 64 = 54$.

cse-1997-b-73.approach: request_R either grants R immediately or records the request. release_R, inside the mutex, hands R directly to the highest-priority recorded requester (V on its semaphore) and keeps busy = true; only if nobody waits does it set busy = false.

steps.title: What release_R must do
steps.body: Waiting processes are blocked on $P(\text{proceed}[p])$ with $R\_requested[p]=\text{true}$. On release, scan priorities $3,2,1$; wake the first requester and clear its flag. The resource passes directly, so **busy stays true**. If no flag is set, set busy := false.

steps.title: Pseudo code
Why it is correct
steps.body: All tests of busy and the flags are inside $P(\text{mutex})\dots V(\text{mutex})$, so a request cannot slip in between the scan and the update. Because busy is never set false while someone is waiting, a newly arriving low-priority process cannot grab R ahead of a waiter, and each waiter is woken in priority order. Priorities are unique, so at most one process waits on each $\text{proceed}[p]$.

answer.value: procedure release_R(priority); P(mutex); if R_requested[3] then begin R_requested[3] := false; V(proceed[3]) end else if R_requested[2] then begin R_requested[2] := false; V(proceed[2]) end else if R_requested[1] then begin R_requested[1] := false; V(proceed[1]) end else busy := false; V(mutex);

pitfalls: Setting busy := false before waking a waiter — a new request could then take R out of priority order.
Forgetting to reset R_requested[p], which would hand R to the same process twice.
Doing the scan outside the mutex (race with request_R).
cse-1997-b-73.verification: Traced: P1 holds R, P2 and P3 request (flags set, both blocked). On P1 release, P3 is woken and busy stays true; on P3 release P2 is woken; on P2 release no flag is set, so busy := false.

pitfalls: Converting the transfer rate wrongly: 3200 B at 800 000 B/s is 4 ms, not 0.4 ms.
Overlapping I/O with processing — without a buffer the program reads, then processes, strictly in sequence.

cse-1997-b-74-b.approach: With one read-ahead buffer, reading record i+1 overlaps processing record i. Reading (14 ms) is slower than processing (3 ms), so the disk is the bottleneck: 1000 reads back to back plus the processing of the last record.
cse-1997-b-74-b.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Records | 1000 × 3200 B |
| Access time | 10 ms |
| Transfer of one record | $3200/(800\times10^3)$ s $=4$ ms |
| CPU per record | 3 ms |

steps.title: Overlap pattern
steps.body: When R1 arrives at 14 ms it is moved to P's variable (negligible time) and the read of R2 starts at once, while the CPU processes R1 (14–17 ms). The CPU then idles until R2 arrives at 28 ms.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
Disk busy continuously: $1000\times14=14000$ ms. The last record is processed after its read: $+3$ ms.

$$14000+3=14003\text{ ms}=14.003\text{ s}\approx14\text{ s}$$

pitfalls: Adding CPU time for every record (17 s) — processing hides behind the next read.
cse-1997-b-74-b.verification: Gantt: reads end at 14, 28, 42 ms …; record k is processed in [14k, 14k+3]; last ends at 14000 + 3.

cse-1997-b-74-c.approach: Blocking factor 2 halves the number of accesses: 500 block reads of 10 + 8 = 18 ms each, overlapped with processing of the previous block (6 ms), plus processing of the last block.
cse-1997-b-74-c.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Records | 1000 × 3200 B |
| Access time | 10 ms |
| Transfer of one record | $3200/(800\times10^3)$ s $=4$ ms |
| CPU per record | 3 ms |

steps.title: One block
steps.body: Block = 2 records = 6400 B. Read: $10+\dfrac{6400}{800\times10^3}\text{ s}=10+8=18$ ms. Processing a block: $2\times3=6$ ms $<18$ ms, so the disk is the bottleneck.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
$1000/2=500$ blocks: $500\times18=9000$ ms, plus processing of the last block $6$ ms.

$$9000+6=9006\text{ ms}=9.006\text{ s}\approx9\text{ s}$$

pitfalls: Paying the 10 ms access per record instead of per block.
Adding only 3 ms at the end — the whole last block (2 records) is processed after the final read.
cse-1997-b-74-c.verification: Reads end at 18, 36, 54 … 9000 ms; the last block is processed 9000–9006 ms.

cse-1997-b-75-a.approach: This is the wound–wait scheme. Show that every wait-for edge goes from a younger process (larger TS) to an older one (smaller TS); timestamps are a strict order, so the wait-for graph can never contain a cycle.

steps.title: Direction of every wait
steps.body: A process P waits only in rule (ii), i.e. when the holder Q has $TS(Q)<TS(P)$. In rule (iii) an older requester never waits — it takes the resource. When a holder releases, the resource goes to the waiter with the smallest TS, so every remaining waiter is younger than the new holder and keeps waiting for an **older** process.

steps.title: No cycle
steps.body: So every edge $P\to Q$ of the wait-for graph satisfies $TS(P)>TS(Q)$. A cycle $P_1\to P_2\to\dots\to P_1$ would need $TS(P_1)>TS(P_2)>\dots>TS(P_1)$ — impossible since timestamps are unique and totally ordered. Hence **deadlock can never arise**.

pitfalls: Confusing with wait–die: here the older process preempts (wounds) the younger holder.
cse-1997-b-75-a.verification: Example: P(TS 1) holds R1, Q(TS 2) holds R2. Q requests R1 → waits (older holder). P requests R2 → Q is restarted, P gets R2. No cycle forms.

cse-1997-b-75-b.approach: A restarted process keeps its timestamp, and new processes get larger timestamps. So a process only ever has finitely many older processes, and once it is the oldest it can never wait or be restarted.

steps.title: The oldest process always finishes
steps.body: Let P have the smallest timestamp in the system. It never waits (no holder is older) and is never restarted (only an older requester can restart it). Since there is no deadlock (part a), it obtains every resource it requests and finishes in finite time.

steps.title: Every process becomes the oldest
steps.body: Timestamps are kept on restart and later arrivals get larger timestamps, so the set of processes older than P is finite and never grows. Each of them finishes in finite time (by induction on timestamp order), after which P is the oldest and finishes too. Hence **no process starves**.

pitfalls: Assuming a restarted process gets a fresh (larger) timestamp — then it could be wounded forever; keeping the old timestamp is exactly what prevents starvation.
cse-1997-b-75-b.verification: A process can be restarted only by strictly older processes, of which there are finitely many, so it can be restarted only finitely often.

cse-1997-b-76-a.approach: Translate SQL directly: FROM → Cartesian product, WHERE → selection, SELECT → projection.

steps.title: Map each clause
steps.body: FROM EMP, INVOLVED $\to EMP\times INVOLVED$; WHERE $\to\sigma_{EMP.eno=INVOLVED.eno\,\wedge\,INVOLVED.pno=3}$; SELECT eno $\to\pi_{eno}$.

steps.title: Expression
steps.body:
$$\pi_{eno}\big(\sigma_{EMP.eno=INVOLVED.eno\ \wedge\ INVOLVED.pno=3}(EMP\times INVOLVED)\big)$$
(Equivalently $\pi_{eno}(\sigma_{pno=3}(INVOLVED))$, since every eno in INVOLVED is also in EMP.)

pitfalls: Using natural join ⋈ — it is not in the allowed operator set {σ, π, ×, ∪, −}.
cse-1997-b-76-a.verification: Each row of the product that survives the selection pairs an employee with one of his rows having pno = 3; projecting eno gives exactly the SQL result.

cse-1997-b-76-b-i.approach: Recognise the standard division pattern: (all employees × all projects) − actual pairs gives the missing pairs; employees with a missing pair are removed.

steps.title: Inner part
steps.body: $\pi_{eno}(INVOLVED)\times\pi_{pno}(PROJ)$ = every (employee, project) combination. Subtracting INVOLVED leaves the pairs where the employee is **not** in that project. $\pi_{eno}$ of that = employees missing at least one project.

steps.title: Outer difference
steps.body: $\pi_{eno}(INVOLVED)$ minus those = employees involved in **every** project, i.e. $INVOLVED\div\pi_{pno}(PROJ)$.

answer.value: Employees (eno) who are involved in every project

pitfalls: Reading it as "employees not in any project" — the subtraction removes only those who miss some project.
cse-1997-b-76-b-i.verification: Example: projects {1, 2}; INVOLVED = {(e1,1),(e1,2),(e2,1)}. Missing pairs {(e2,2)} → result {e1}, the only employee in all projects.

cse-1997-b-76-b-ii.approach: Read the second term as $\pi_{E.age}(\sigma_{E.age<EMP.age}(\rho_E(EMP)\times EMP))$: the ages that are smaller than some other age. Subtracting them from all ages leaves the largest age.

steps.title: Interpret the printed expression
steps.body: The subscript $E.age<EMP.age$ is a selection condition on $\rho_E(EMP)\times EMP$ (the paper merges $\sigma$ into $\pi$). The pairs kept are those where the copy's age is less than some employee's age; the projected ages are therefore the **non-maximum** ages.

steps.title: Difference
steps.body: $\pi_{age}(EMP)$ − (ages that are less than some other age) = ages not less than any age = the **maximum age**, i.e. the age of the oldest employee(s).

answer.value: The maximum age among employees (age of the oldest employee)

pitfalls: Projecting EMP.age instead of E.age would remove the non-minimum ages and give the minimum — the projected attribute is E.age.
cse-1997-b-76-b-ii.verification: Ages {25, 30, 40}: ages smaller than some other = {25, 30}; difference = {40}, the maximum.
